newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales grow 4.3 percent in February - BRC.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales grow 4.3 percent in February - BRC.

text.p: Retail sales in Britain grew 4.3 percent in February on a like-for-like basis compared with a year earlier, down from 4.9 percent in January, but the underlying growth rate remains broadly stable, the British Retail Consortium (BRC) said.
Its retail sales monitor showed an average rate of increase over the last three months of 4.6 percent compared with 4.7 percent in the three months to January.

"The underlying growth of sales values has dropped back significantly from the 6.5 percent recorded last August, though this has been a period of falling inflation in the prices of retailed goods, particularly in the food sector," the BRC said.
In January, retail goods prices were up 1.7 percent from a year earlier, while the overall RPI rose 2.8 percent.
Non-food sales continued their relatively strong performance in February while a major fall in prices of fresh produce resulted in only modest gains in the value of food sales.
The BRC described the strong pound as a two-edged sword, "keeping prices down but also keeping tourists away."
Andrew Higginson, chairman of the BRC economic affairs committee, said the figures showed retailing maintaining steady, healthy growth.
"The market remains extremely competitive, with the strong pound and value-conscious consumers keeping any prices rises to a minimum," he said.

Andrew Sentance, the BRC's chief economic adviser, said lower inflation in the retail sector, especially in food, had been a major factor contributing to the fallback in the growth of retail sales values since last summer.
"With the pound remaining strong, this downward pressure on prices is likely to continue, which should bring inflation back within its target range of below 2.5 percent later this year," he said.
The February survey covered the four weeks from February 2 to March 1.
